lessons.title: Identifying high-yielding mother trees in your community
lessons.body: Your first job is to find a mother tree that gives you the best possible scion wood. A mother tree is any healthy tree you take cuttings from. It must be high-yielding, disease-free, and true to type. In your community, start by asking farmers which mango, avocado, or citrus tree gives the most fruit every year. Visit that tree during harvest. Look for a tree that has produced heavily for at least three years. Count the fruit on a few branches. A good mango mother tree might carry 200 to 300 fruits in a good season. Check the fruit size and taste. Avoid trees with small, fibrous, or diseased fruit. Also check for pests and diseases. Look for signs of anthracnose (black spots on leaves and fruit), gummosis (sticky sap on the trunk), or viral diseases like tristeza in citrus. Do not take scion wood from a tree with these problems. The tree should be at least five years old and in full production. Young trees may not have stable genetics. Also, avoid trees that have been heavily pruned or stressed by drought. The best mother trees are vigorous, with strong new growth. Look for branches that are exposed to sunlight, as they produce healthier wood. In Africa, many good mother trees are found in home gardens or old orchards. Ask around, and mark the tree with a ribbon or paint so you can return. Never take all your scion wood from one tree; collect from two or three good trees to spread risk. This simple selection process is the foundation of a successful orchard.

lessons.title: When and how to cut scion wood for maximum success
lessons.body: Timing is critical. Cut scion wood when the tree is dormant or just before bud break. In most of Africa, the best time is the cool dry season, from June to August in southern Africa, or December to February in West Africa. Avoid cutting during active growth, flowering, or fruiting. The wood should be mature but not old. Choose branches from the current season's growth that are about the thickness of a pencil (6-10 mm diameter). They should have well-developed buds. Use a sharp, clean pair of bypass pruners or a grafting knife. Make a clean cut 30-40 cm long. Cut just above a bud at the top and just below a bud at the bottom. Remove any leaves immediately, but leave a short piece of leaf stalk (petiole) to protect the bud. Do not strip the bark. Cut more wood than you need, as some may dry out or get damaged. For mango, cut 20-30 cm long scions; for citrus, 15-20 cm. After cutting, tie the scions in bundles of 5-10 with the buds pointing in the same direction. Label each bundle with the variety name and date. Wrap the bundles in moist newspaper or banana leaves, then place in a plastic bag. Do not seal the bag completely; leave a small opening for air. Keep them cool and out of direct sun. If you are cutting from a tall tree, use a pole pruner or climb safely. Never cut from the top of the tree where wood may be too soft. Cut from the outer canopy where light is good. The best scions come from branches that are 1-2 years old. Avoid water sprouts (vertical shoots) as they are often too soft. With practice, you will learn to identify the perfect wood.

lessons.title: Storing and transporting scion wood without drying out
lessons.body: Scion wood is alive and must not dry out. After cutting, you have about 24-48 hours to use it, but proper storage can extend that to 2-3 weeks. The key is to keep it cool and moist, but not wet. Wrap the bundles in slightly moist (not dripping) newspaper, then place them in a perforated plastic bag. Store in a refrigerator at 4-8Â°C if you have one. If not, find the coolest place in your house, like a clay pot with a lid, or a hole in the ground shaded by a tree. You can also bury the bundles in damp sand or sawdust. For transport, use a cooler box with a little ice in a separate container, or wrap in wet cloth and carry in a shaded bag. Never leave scions in a hot car or in direct sun. If you are traveling long distances, check them every few hours. If the newspaper dries, re-moisten it lightly. Do not soak the wood in water; that causes rot. Also, do not store scions with ripe fruit, as ethylene gas from fruit can damage the buds. Label each bundle clearly with a permanent marker on a plastic tag. Include the variety, date, and location. If you are collecting multiple varieties, keep them separate to avoid mixing. When you are ready to graft, remove the bundles from storage and let them come to room temperature for an hour before grafting. Inspect the wood: it should be green under the bark and the buds should be plump. If the wood is brown and dry, it is dead. With proper storage, you can collect scions from a distant mother tree and still achieve high graft success.

lessons.title: Labeling and tracking different varieties
lessons.body: If you are collecting scions from more than one tree, you must label them correctly. Mixing up varieties leads to wasted grafts and confusion in your orchard. Use durable labels. Plastic tags with a hole punched in them work well. Write with a permanent marker or a pencil. Include the variety name (e.g., 'Apple Mango', 'Hass Avocado'), the date collected, and the mother tree's location or a code. If you don't know the variety name, give it a local name like 'Mama Jane's Mango'. Attach one label to each bundle. Also, write the same information on a piece of paper and keep it in your record book. As you graft, keep a map of your orchard. Draw a simple diagram showing which variety is grafted on which rootstock. Number each tree. For example, Tree 1: 'Apple Mango' on local rootstock. This helps you track performance later. If you sell scions or share with neighbors, give them a copy of the label. In Africa, many farmers lose track of varieties and end up with poor quality fruit. Labeling solves that. Use a pencil on plastic because marker can fade in the sun. If you are collecting from wild trees, note the fruit characteristics: size, color, taste, season. That way, even without a name, you can identify the best ones. Keep your labels with the scions during storage and transport. When grafting, double-check the label before making the cut. A simple mistake like swapping labels can ruin a year's work. Also, keep a notebook with dates of grafting, budding, and first harvest. This record becomes valuable for future planning.

lessons.title: Avoiding disease transfer when collecting scions
lessons.body: Diseases can spread from the mother tree to your orchard through scion wood. The most common are viruses, bacteria, and fungi. For example, citrus tristeza virus, mango bacterial black spot, and avocado sunblotch viroid can all be carried in scions. To avoid this, only collect from trees that look healthy. Inspect the leaves, branches, and trunk for symptoms: yellowing, mottling, cankers, gumming, or dieback. If you see any signs, do not take wood from that tree. Even if the tree looks healthy, it might be a carrier. The safest approach is to collect from trees that have been certified disease-free, but in most African communities, such certification is rare. So, use your eyes and ask local extension officers. Also, sterilize your tools between trees. Use a 10% bleach solution or rubbing alcohol (70%) to wipe your pruners and knife. Dip the blades for 30 seconds. This prevents moving pathogens from one tree to another. When cutting, avoid touching the cut surface with your hands. Wear clean gloves if possible. After collecting, do not store scions with any diseased plant material. If you see any rot or mold on the scions during storage, discard them immediately. When grafting, make sure your rootstock is also healthy. A weak rootstock can become infected. In some cases, you can hot-water treat scions (50Â°C for 10 minutes) to kill some pathogens, but this is tricky and can damage the buds. Better to start clean. Remember, once a virus is in your orchard, it is almost impossible to remove. So, prevention is everything. Collect from the best, healthiest trees, and keep your tools clean.

lessons.title: Hands-on: Collecting and preparing scions from a local mango tree
lessons.body: Now let's put it all into practice. You will need: a sharp grafting knife or bypass pruners, a clean cloth, 70% alcohol, plastic tags, a permanent marker, moist newspaper, a plastic bag, and a cooler box. Choose a healthy mango tree that has produced well for at least three years. Go to the tree in the early morning when it is cool. Look for branches that are about the thickness of a pencil, with plump buds. These are usually in the outer canopy, exposed to sun. Cut 30 cm long scions. Make a clean cut just above a bud at the top, and just below a bud at the bottom. Remove the leaves but leave a short petiole. Cut 10-15 scions from different parts of the tree. As you cut, place them in a bundle with buds pointing up. After cutting, sterilize your knife with alcohol. Then, take a bundle and wrap it in slightly moist newspaper. Write a label: 'Mango - [local name] - [date] - [tree location]'. Attach the label to the bundle. Place the bundle in a plastic bag and tie it loosely. Put the bag in your cooler box with a small ice pack wrapped in a cloth. Do not let the ice touch the scions. If you are grafting the same day, keep them in the shade. If you are storing, put them in a refrigerator at 4-8Â°C. Before grafting, inspect each scion: the bark should be green when scratched, and buds should be firm. Discard any that are dry or brown. Now you are ready to graft. This hands-on practice will teach you the importance of speed, cleanliness, and care. Repeat this process with other fruit trees like avocado or citrus. The more you practice, the better your success rate.

quiz.q: What is a mother tree?
options: A) A tree that produces flowers
B) A tree from which you collect scion wood
C) A tree that is very old
D) A tree that has no fruit
quiz.explanation: A mother tree is the source of scion wood for grafting.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a good mother tree for mango?
options: A) It has small, fibrous fruit
B) It has black spots on leaves
C) It has produced heavily for at least three years
D) It is less than two years old
quiz.explanation: A high-yielding tree with a history of good production is ideal.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid taking scion wood from a tree with gummosis?
options: A) The wood is too soft
B) The disease can spread to your orchard
C) The tree is too young
D) The fruit will be too small
quiz.explanation: Gummosis is a disease that can be transmitted through scion wood.

quiz.q: What is the best time to cut scion wood in most of Africa?
options: B) When the tree is flowering
C) During the cool dry season
quiz.explanation: Dormant or just before bud break is best, which occurs in the cool dry season.

quiz.q: What diameter should scion wood ideally be?
quiz.explanation: Pencil-thick wood (6-10 mm) is mature enough but still flexible.

quiz.q: How long should mango scions be?
quiz.explanation: Mango scions are typically 20-30 cm long for easy handling.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after cutting scion wood?
options: C) Leave it in the sun
quiz.explanation: Leaves transpire and cause drying; remove them but keep a short petiole.

quiz.q: Why should you not seal the plastic bag completely when storing scions?
quiz.explanation: Some air exchange prevents buildup of moisture and rot.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for scion wood?
quiz.explanation: Cool but not freezing temperatures slow down respiration without damaging buds.

quiz.q: How long can properly stored scions last?
quiz.explanation: With proper cool, moist storage, scions can remain viable for 2-3 weeks.

quiz.q: What should you do if the newspaper wrapping dries out during storage?
quiz.explanation: Light re-moistening maintains humidity without causing rot.

quiz.q: Why should you not store scions with ripe fruit?
options: B) Fruit produces ethylene gas that damages buds
C) Fruit makes them too wet
quiz.explanation: Ethylene gas from ripe fruit can cause bud abscission and reduce viability.

quiz.q: What information should a scion label include?
options: A) Variety name, date, and location
quiz.explanation: These details help track variety and collection date.

quiz.q: Why is labeling important when collecting multiple varieties?
options: A) To make the bundle look nice
B) To avoid mixing up varieties
quiz.explanation: Mixing varieties leads to confusion and loss of desired traits.

quiz.q: What is a good alternative if you don't know the variety name?
options: B) Give it a local name
quiz.explanation: A local name helps you remember the source and characteristics.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a record of grafting dates and varieties?
options: B) To track performance and plan future grafts
quiz.explanation: Records help you learn which varieties perform best and when to harvest.

quiz.q: Which disease can be spread through citrus scion wood?
quiz.explanation: Citrus tristeza virus is a major concern and is graft-transmissible.

quiz.q: How can you sterilize your pruning tools between trees?
options: B) Dip in 10% bleach or 70% alcohol
quiz.explanation: Bleach or alcohol kills pathogens on blades.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mold on stored scions?
options: D) Cut off the moldy part
quiz.explanation: Mold indicates decay and the scions are likely dead or diseased.

quiz.q: Why is it important to collect scions from the outer canopy?
options: A) They are easier to reach
B) They have better light exposure and are healthier
quiz.explanation: Sun-exposed branches produce more vigorous and productive scions.

quiz.q: What tool is best for cutting scion wood?
options: B) A sharp grafting knife or bypass pruners
quiz.explanation: Sharp, clean cuts heal faster and reduce disease entry.

quiz.q: How many scions should you cut from a single tree?
quiz.explanation: Cutting 10-15 allows for selection and backup, but avoid over-harvesting.

quiz.q: What should you do before grafting stored scions?
options: B) Let them come to room temperature
quiz.explanation: Gradual warming prevents shock and improves graft success.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign that a scion is dead?
quiz.explanation: Brown, dry wood indicates the scion is no longer alive.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid water sprouts for scion wood?
options: A) They are too soft and have poor buds
quiz.explanation: Water sprouts are vigorous but often have poor carbohydrate reserves and buds.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the hands-on activity?
quiz.explanation: Sterilizing tools prevents disease transmission before cutting.

quiz.q: How should you carry scions during transport?
options: A) In an open basket in sun
B) In a cooler box with ice pack wrapped
D) In a bucket of water
quiz.explanation: Cool, moist, shaded conditions keep scions alive.

quiz.q: What should you write on the label for a hands-on collection?
options: B) Variety, date, and tree location
quiz.explanation: Complete information ensures traceability.

quiz.q: Why is it important to collect scions in the early morning?
options: A) It is cooler and scions are hydrated
B) Trees are easier to climb
C) Buds are easier to see
quiz.explanation: Cooler temperatures reduce water loss and stress on scions.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot graft immediately after collecting?
options: A) Leave them in the sun
B) Store them properly in cool, moist conditions
quiz.explanation: Proper storage maintains viability until grafting.
